attachment.content:
- adr-authoring: Create or edit architecture decision records with clear scope, evidence, alternatives, consequences, review traceability, and editable architecture diagrams. Use when drafting, reviewing, or updating an ADR or deciding whether a change needs one.
- captions-overlay: Overlay doctrine for the embedded-captions workflow — the caption MODEL (drop / rail / embed) and the rule that captions are an OVERLAY composited on top of the film, never a reserved bottom band you shift content up to avoid. Load when adding captions/subtitles to a talking-head or launch video, when deciding whether a phrase should be dropped, ride the verbatim rail, or be promoted to a scarce embedded climax, when laying out a composition that will carry captions (do NOT reserve a keep-out band), or when centering a composition on the true frame center under captions. Quotes the rail+embed model from embedded-captions and constraint
- caveman: Ultra-compressed communication mode. Cuts token usage ~75% by dropping filler, articles, and pleasantries while keeping full technical accuracy. Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", or invokes /caveman.
- changelog-video: Turn a weekly changelog .md into a finished branded changelog video (square 1080, ~45-60s, Annie VO, animated brand background, mock-UI visualizations, lowkey captions). Use when the user provides a changelog/digest markdown and wants the weekly video, or says "changelog video". Self-contained — fonts, background, lexicon, and scripts ship in this skill.
- code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".
- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- create-goal-prompt: Creates concise, execution-ready goal prompts from task context, with explicit scope, constraints, deliverables, acceptance criteria, verification, and completion conditions. Use when the user asks to turn notes, a ticket, a specification, or a rough request into a prompt for Codex, Claude Code, or another agent; asks to improve a task prompt; or needs testable acceptance criteria for an autonomous task.
- cut-the-curve: The technique catalog: five velocity-matched SEAMS (zoom-through, INVERSE zoom-through, cut-the-curve, waterfall cut, rack-focus blur-cut) plus the two in-scene techniques — waterfall ENTRY (staggered arrival cascades for title cards / segment openers) and the nudge curve (slow-fast-slow three-phase group slides). Covers partial-travel (~12% of frame) velocity matching via mirrored power4 eases, the Z scale-sign rule, size-scaled blur (10px text / 18-20px full-frame), word-by-word staggered cuts, cascade pacing by element weight, and the 10/65/25 slide ratio. Read before authoring any transition, text-beat handoff, kinetic text entry, or group reposition. [depth, zoom, inverse-zoom, scale-sign, mirrored-zoom, rack-focus, pacing, velocity, cut-the-curve, waterfall, stagger, cascade, kinetic-text, title-card, segment-opener, nudge, slide, easing, group-motion, z-depth, motion-graphics, cinematic, transition, blur, directional-continuity]
- diagnose: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. Use when user says "diagnose this" / "debug this", reports a bug, says something is broken/throwing/failing, or describes a performance regression.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- do-issues: Fetch ready-for-agent Jira tickets and implement them in parallel using subagents. Each ticket gets its own git worktree, branch, and MR. Use when user says "do issues", "work on tickets", "implement ready tickets", or invokes /do-issues.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when discussing codebase terminology, writing or editing a CONTEXT.md, or recording or editing an ADR.
- embedded-captions: Add captions or subtitles to an existing single-subject talking-head video without editing the footage. Use for plain verbatim captions, cinematic captions embedded behind the subject, VFX captions, “炸/特效/酷炫字幕,” or a named identity from the 35-style catalog. Route by visual identity, not by backend engine. The quiet `anchor` rail is the default; embed every word only when the user explicitly wants a fully cinematic treatment. The workflow runs locally end to end, including transcription and subject matting; split multi-shot footage before applying it.
- faceless-explainer: Turn arbitrary text — an article, notes, a topic, a brief — into a faceless explainer video: there is no site or footage to capture, so the visuals are invented per scene (typography, abstract graphics, diagrams, data-viz). Use for topic explainers, concept breakdowns, how-tos, listicles. Not a video built from a website (/product-launch-video — promo or tour). Unclear → /hyperframes.
- figma: Import Figma content into a HyperFrames composition — rendered assets, brand tokens, components, storyboard sections → reconstructed motion (frames read as states, not slides) (REST/CLI), connector-assisted motion when available, and shaders from a connector or native export. Use when the user pastes a figma.com link or asks to bring a Figma design, frame, logo, brand, or animation into a video/composition.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. # User-Level Claude Instructions

These instructions apply globally across all projects and sessions.

## Planning

For config changes, integrations, and multi-step tasks: outline the plan in 3-5 bullet points and wait for approval before executing.

## Accuracy

When referencing project-specific implementations (metrics, migrations, configs), always verify claims against actual source code before stating something is 'implemented' or 'completed'. Never infer work status from metadata alone.

When asked about implementation status or what's been done, grep/read the actual source files to verify before answering. Don't infer from commit messages or ticket status alone.

## MCP Setup

Config file: `~/.claude/mcp.json`

| Server | Transport | Auth | Notes |
|--------|-----------|------|-------|
| **GitLab** (`plugin_development_gitlab`) | `npx mcp-remote` → `https://gitlab.loc/api/v4/mcp` | OAuth (managed by mcp-remote, token in `~/.bashrc`) | Requires custom CA: `~/.config/xsolla/ca.crt` via `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`. Do NOT use PAT auth. |
| **Datadog** | `npx datadog-mcp-server` | API key + App key in env | Site: `us5.datadoghq.com`. Keys in `~/.claude/mcp.json`. |
| **claude-mem** | Plugin (thedotmack marketplace) | None | Persistent cross-session memory. Use `mcp__plugin_claude-mem_mcp-search__*` tools. |
| **Atlassian** (×2) | Claude.ai integration | OAuth | Two instances (`Atlassian` + `Atlassian_2`) — use either, they're identical. Covers Jira + Confluence. |
| **Slack** | Claude.ai integration | OAuth | `mcp__claude_ai_Slack__*` tools. |
| **Gmail / GCal** | Claude.ai integration | OAuth | Standard Google workspace tools. |
| **Xsolla MCP** | Claude.ai integration | Internal | `mcp__claude_ai_Xsolla_MCP__*` — ask_xsolla_question, search_xsolla_sources. |

**Known gotchas:**
- GitLab MCP auth errors: check that mcp-remote OAuth token is valid (re-auth via browser if needed)
- Dual Atlassian instances sometimes open duplicate browser tabs — normal, ignore
- `datadog-mcp-server` keys in `~/.claude/mcp.json` are **different** from the Datadog API/App keys used for direct API calls (those are in project memory)

## Communication Style

When drafting messages, MR comments, or replies for the user, use a natural, conversational tone. Avoid robotic or overly formal language. Match the user's communication style.

Never use the em dash character (—). Rewrite sentences to avoid needing it. Use commas, periods, parentheses, or just split into separate sentences instead.

## Endpoint Discovery

Before generating configs for external services (Datadog synthetics, health checks, API integrations): probe actual endpoints first with curl/Bash to verify they exist and return expected status codes. Never assume endpoint paths — common variants differ per service (`/health`, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/api/v2/readyz`, `/api/v1/health`). Generate configs only against verified endpoints. Call out any required manual steps (e.g. private locations) explicitly before presenting output.

## Git Workflow

Only push/commit files explicitly requested. Do not include extra files in commits or pushes without explicit confirmation.

## Claude Init Settings
role=developer


## IMPORTANT: Xsolla code search (Neuronet MCP)
Before your first Grep/Glob/multi-file Read in any task that involves
locating, understanding, or explaining code you didn't just create or
aren't already looking at: see `rules/neo4j-graph-first.md`. Your first move
must be an actual call to `neuronet_code_search` — not a check of whether
it's available, an actual call. Only if that call fails or the tool isn't in
your tool list, fall back to normal file search — silently, no prompts, no
asking to authorize anything. Delegating to a subagent (Task/Agent, incl.
Explore/Plan)? It won't inherit this — paste the check into its prompt as
text yourself.

# Xsolla code search — use Neuronet Code Search, not grep

**MANDATORY, before your first `Grep`/`Glob`/multi-file `Read` in any task
that involves locating, understanding, or explaining code you didn't just
create or aren't already looking at**: your first move must be an actual
call to `neuronet_code_search` — not a check of whether it's listed in your
tools, an actual `action=search` call with a scoped query derived from the
task. Don't reason about availability in the abstract; attempt the call and
see what happens.

- **Tool name**: `neuronet_code_search` (from the "Neuronet" MCP server —
  in Claude Code this shows up as `mcp__claude_ai_Neuronet__neuronet_code_search`
  or similar, depending on connector naming). Don't match on the exact
  prefix — look for a `neuronet_code_search` tool from a Neuronet MCP.
- **Call succeeds?** Use it for the rest of this session's code search
  instead of `Grep`/`Glob`/broad `Read`. See workflow below.
- **Call fails, or the tool isn't in your tool list at all?** *Then* fall
  back to normal file search for the rest of the session — silently, no
  prompts, no asking the user to authorize anything, no need to mention it
  unless they ask. Don't pretend to have searched via Neuronet.

**Delegating to a subagent (Task/Agent tool, incl. Explore/Plan)?** Subagents
do not automatically inherit this file. If the task you're delegating
involves locating or explaining code, paste this whole check directly into
the subagent's prompt as text — don't assume it already knows this.

## Tool reference

`neuronet_code_search` actions:

- `search` — lexical (BM25) search over indexed source. `query` is matched
  **literally**, not semantically — use exact terms/identifiers, not
  paraphrases. `mode: "content"` (default) searches chunk content; `mode:
  "path"` searches file paths instead. Optional filters: `repo` (exact repo
  name), `provider` (`github`|`gitlab`), `ref` (branch), `path` (substring),
  `limit`.
- `list_repositories` — which repos are indexed; pass `query` to filter by
  repo name. Use this once per new repo to confirm it's indexed before
  relying on search results being complete — if a repo you're working in
  isn't listed, its code isn't indexed and search results for it will be
  empty or absent (not an error, just no coverage).
- `get_file` — reconstructs a full file from its indexed chunks. Requires
  `repo` + `path`. Prefer reading the real file from the local working tree
  for anything you're about to edit (see Freshness below); use `get_file`
  only when you don't have local disk access to that repo/path.

## Workflow: search -> expand

1. **SEARCH**: call `search` with a scoped `query` (add `repo`/`path` filters
   when known) instead of grepping the repo yourself.
2. **EXPAND**: for the top few distinct hits, open the exact file at the
   exact `path`/`startLine`/`endLine` from the local working tree — don't
   dump whole files or whole directories when you already have the specific
   location.

## Freshness caveat

The index can lag the current branch/commit. Use it to FIND, then always
confirm the exact current code on disk before editing — don't trust
`get_file`'s reconstructed content as ground truth for anything you're about
to change.

# xsolla-ai-kit — Agent Context

This file is read automatically by most AI coding agents (Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Amp, Devin, Jules, Aider, Roo Code, Augment). Claude Code users: `CLAUDE.md` is a copy of this file.

---

## What this repo is

`xsolla/xsolla-ai-kit` is the Xsolla agent skills toolkit — a collection of `SKILL.md` files (agentskills.io format) that teach AI coding agents how to execute Xsolla-specific workflows end-to-end, without requiring the Xsolla CLI as a dependency.

Skills call **Xsolla REST APIs directly**. The CLI (`xsolla/xsolla-cli`) is an optional shortcut once it ships to production.

---

## Skill inventory

| Skill                           | What it does                                                                             |
|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `shop-setup`                    | **Orchestrator** — coordinates the full zero-to-shop flow, chaining all domain skills    |
| `merchant-setup`                | Creates and configures an Xsolla account + get API key                                   |
| `catalog-design`                | Configures the catalog and the client flow: client catalog, purchase, order confirmation |
| `login-setup`                   | Integrates Xsolla Login / NewID authentication                                           |
| `login-styling`                 | Applies a custom visual style / theme / brand to the Login UI (pairs with `login-setup`) |
| `headless-checkout-integration` | Payments via Headless Checkout                                                           |
| `webhooks-impl`                 | Generates webhook handler code for order/payment events                                  |
| `quest-setup`                   | Creates and manages Quest Platform quests, events and rewards                            |
| `production`                    | Sandbox → live: contract, flip flags, deploy, developer live-payment checklist           |

---

## How to invoke a skill

Skills are loaded automatically when you open this repo in your agent. To run a specific skill, ask your agent naturally:

```
Set up a full Xsolla game shop for my project
→ triggers: shop-setup

Configure my Xsolla catalog with items and pricing
→ triggers: catalog-design

Integrate payments into my game
→ triggers: headless-checkout-integration

Go live / leave sandbox
→ triggers: production

Create a quest that rewards players
→ triggers: quest-setup
```

---

## Environment variables

```bash
XSOLLA_MERCHANT_ID=<your merchant ID>
XSOLLA_PROJECT_ID=<your project ID>
XSOLLA_PROJECT_API_KEY=<your API key>
```
Setup by `merchant-setup` skill.

For Quest Platform only, the optional `XSOLLA_QP_ENV` selector defaults to
`production`; set it to `stage` only for an explicit controlled stage run. It
is a service selector, not a credential. Keep it when updating merchant

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

## Establish Shared Understanding

The outcome of brainstorming is an understanding your human partner can
recognize and correct, grounded in what they want to accomplish.

1. **Discover intent.** Use the request and available context to identify
   the intended outcome, who it is for, and what success looks like. When
   that information is missing, ask one focused question about purpose or
   intended use before proposing features or an approach. Knowing the app
   genre does not tell you why your partner wants it. Gathering missing
   requirements does not ask them to authorize the task again.
2. **Write back your understanding.** Summarize the intended outcome,
   relevant constraints, and success criteria in a short note your partner
   can assess. Separate what they said from assumptions. Invite correction
   and incorporate their answer before treating this as the design brief.
3. **Carry intent into the design.** Preserve the agreed understanding in
   the selected path's design artifact: the written spec for architectural
   work, or the in-chat design/probe for bounded work and spikes. Check
   proposed features and technical choices against that understanding.

When the request already supplies the purpose and constraints, reflect
that understanding instead of asking the same questions again. Keep the
note concise; its accuracy and the opportunity to correct it matter.

<HARD-GATE>
Before taking any implementation action, including invoking an
implementation skill, writing product code, scaffolding, installing
product dependencies, or creating an external project, complete the
selected path's prerequisites:

- Spike: the human partner approves the question and probe.
- Bounded: the human partner approves the short in-chat design.
- Architectural: the human partner reviews and approves the written spec,
  then reviews the written implementation plan and selects its execution
  method. Conversational design approval only permits writing the spec;
  written-spec approval only permits invoking writing-plans.

A reply approves the stage actually presented. Approval of an idea or
feature scope does not approve artifacts that do not exist yet. Resume
at the earliest incomplete stage; do not turn one approval into permission
to skip the rest of the selected path. Read-only project exploration is
allowed while those prerequisites remain incomplete.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving the required design
before implementation. A bounded change may need only two sentences in
chat. A new todo-list project is architectural and requires the written
spec and planning handoffs. Scale the artifact to the selected path;
complete that path's reviews before implementation.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Follow the selected path: a bounded change gets a short chat design; an architectural change gets the written spec and planning handoffs. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:

schema.description:

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

1	# Voidwall — agent context pack
2	
3	This file is the single source of truth for an AI agent building a live Xsolla web shop for the fictional game *Voidwall*, by the fictional studio *Meridian Foundry*. Hand it to an agent together with the Xsolla CLI.
4	
5	## How to use this file
6	
7	This pack carries the decisions and data for the store: the studio, the game, the catalog, prices, and the project configuration. The agent already has the Xsolla CLI for command syntax, so this file stays focused on what to build rather than how to call it.
8	
9	The agent's job: read this pack, then use the CLI to create the project, configure login and payments, build the catalog (currency, items, bundles, subscriptions), wire webhooks, and stand up the storefront. The build checklist at the end maps every section here to the Xsolla setup phases.
10	
11	Image assets (item icons, currency icons, backgrounds, key art, logo) live in `./assets/` and are referenced by filename throughout. When an asset is missing, the agent should leave the image field unset and flag it.
12	
13	Everything below is fiction. Use placeholder values for anything legal, financial, or personally identifying.
14	
15	## The studio: Meridian Foundry
16	
17	- **Studio name:** Meridian Foundry
18	- **Legal entity:** Meridian Foundry, Lda. (placeholder)
19	- **Headquarters:** Lisbon, Portugal
20	- **Founded:** 2021
21	- **Team size:** ~28 people
22	- **Website:** meridianfoundry.com
23	- **Catalog:** *Voidwall* is the studio's second title. Their first was a smaller mobile roguelike.
24	- **Support email:** support@playvoidwall.com
25	- **Brand voice:** confident, technical, a little grim. The studio talks to players like fellow engineers holding a line.
26	
27	## The game: Voidwall
28	
29	**Genre:** Sci-fi tower defense
30	**Platforms:** Windows (Steam, Epic Games Store), macOS, iOS, Android
31	**Player site / store domain:** playvoidwall.com
32	
33	### Premise and setting
34	
35	Humanity's expansion has stalled at the **Frontier**, the ragged edge of charted space. Out there drift the **Wells**: derelict alien megastructures that periodically wake and flood nearby colonies with the **Rime**, a self-replicating machine swarm that freezes and consumes everything it reaches.
36	
37	Players are **Wardens**: engineers who deploy and upgrade automated turret networks across orbital platforms and colony hulls to hold the line through escalating Rime waves. The turret line players build is called the **Voidwall**.
38	
39	### Core gameplay loop
40	
41	1. Deploy turrets onto fixed **hardpoints** across a map.
42	2. Manage a **power budget**, since every turret draws energy.
43	3. Survive escalating waves of Rime.
44	4. Earn **Scrap** (soft currency) from kills and completed waves.
45	5. Spend Scrap and **Cores** (premium currency) to unlock, upgrade, and customize turrets between waves and runs.
46	
47	### Turret classes
48	
49	Six classes anchor the economy. Players unlock and field the classes through gameplay; the classes themselves are never sold. The store sells **cosmetic skins** that re-dress a class a player already fields. Skins change appearance only and carry no stat or gameplay effect, so the store stays cosmetic-only and non-pay-to-win. Each skin is its own SKU.
50	
51	| Class | Role |
52	|-------|------|
53	| **Spitter** | Rapid kinetic, low cost, anti-swarm |
54	| **Arclight** | Chain lightning, hits multiple linked targets |
55	| **Bulwark** | Slow heavy cannon, high single-target damage |
56	| **Hailstorm** | Flak burst, area denial |
57	| **Lancer** | Long-range railgun, anti-armor sniper |
58	| **Tether** | Support field, slows and weakens enemies in range |
59	
60	### Art direction (for asset generation)
61	
62	Use this when generating or selecting store assets so everything stays consistent.
63	
64	- **Palette:**
65	  - Void black `#0A0E14` (backgrounds)
66	  - Hull steel `#2A3242` (panels, structures)
67	  - Cyan energy `#35E0FF` (friendly weapons, UI accent)
68	  - Plasma white `#EAF6FF` (highlights, weapon glow)
69	  - Warning amber `#FFA63D` (alerts, legendary rarity)
70	  - Rime violet `#8B6CFF` (the enemy swarm)
71	- **Style:** clean hard-surface sci-fi, physically based rendering for in-game objects; painterly, high-contrast key art for promo. Cold, industrial, lit by weapon glow against deep space.
72	- **Item icons:** the item centered on a dark hexagonal tile, with a rarity-colored rim glow. Common gray, Rare blue, Epic purple, Legendary amber.
73	- **Logo:** wordmark `VOIDWALL` in a geometric industrial face, paired with a shield/wall glyph formed from hexagons.
74	- **Typography:** geometric industrial sans for display; clean humanist sans for body.
75	
76	## The store
77	
78	Premium currency is **Cores**, bought with real money. Soft currency is **Scrap**, earned in-game. Scrap is listed here only so the agent models it and keeps it out of the storefront.
79	
80	### Item groups (catalog structure)
81	
82	Create these groups in display order:
83	
84	1. **Currency** — Core packages
85	2. **Turret Skins** — cosmetic skins per turret class
86	3. **Warden Gear** — player avatar cosmetics, emotes, decals
87	4. **Boosters** — consumable progression boosts
88	5. **Bundles** — multi-item value packs
89	6. **Passes and Subscriptions** — battle pass and recurring membership
90	
91	### Currencies
92	
93	| Currency | SKU | Type | Sold? | Image |
94	|----------|-----|------|-------|-------|
95	| Cores | `cores` | Premium (hard) | Yes, via packages | `assets/currency/cores\.jpg` |
96	| Scrap | `scrap` | Soft (earned) | No | `assets/currency/scrap\.jpg` |
97	
98	### Virtual currency packages (Cores, real money)
99	
100	All in group **Currency**. Prices in USD; set regional pricing per the Localization section.
101	
102	| Package | SKU | Cores (base + bonus = total) | Price USD | Image |
103	|---------|-----|------------------------------|-----------|-------|
104	| Core Cache | `cores_500` | 500 + 0 = 500 | 4.99 | `assets/currency/pack_cache\.jpg` |
105	| Core Stack | `cores_1200` | 1,100 + 100 = 1,200 | 9.99 | `assets/currency/pack_stack\.jpg` |

108	| Core Reactor | `cores_15000` | 11,500 + 3,500 = 15,000 | 99.99 | `assets/currency/pack_reactor\.jpg` |
109	
110	### Virtual items: turret skins (priced in Cores)
111	
112	Group **Turret Skins**. Image path pattern: `assets/skins/<sku>\.jpg`.
113	
114	| Name | SKU | Class | Rarity | Price (Cores) |
115	|------|-----|-------|--------|---------------|
116	| Obsidian | `spitter_skin_obsidian` | Spitter | Rare | 800 |
117	| Huntsman | `spitter_skin_huntsman` | Spitter | Epic | 1,500 |
118	| Voltaic | `arclight_skin_voltaic` | Arclight | Rare | 800 |

120	| Ironclad | `bulwark_skin_ironclad` | Bulwark | Rare | 800 |
121	| Warlord | `bulwark_skin_warlord` | Bulwark | Epic | 1,500 |
122	| Frostbite | `hailstorm_skin_frostbite` | Hailstorm | Epic | 1,500 |
123	| Tempest | `hailstorm_skin_tempest` | Hailstorm | Legendary | 2,400 |
124	| Longshot | `lancer_skin_longshot` | Lancer | Rare | 800 |
125	| Deadeye | `lancer_skin_deadeye` | Lancer | Legendary | 2,400 |
126	| Anchor | `tether_skin_anchor` | Tether | Rare | 800 |
127	
128	Set a custom attribute on each skin: `rarity` and `turret_class`.
129	
130	### Virtual items: Warden gear (priced in Cores)
131	
132	Group **Warden Gear**.
133	
134	| Name | SKU | Type | Price (Cores) |
135	|------|-----|------|---------------|
136	| Frontier Issue | `warden_armor_frontier` | Armor (Common) | 400 |
137	| Vanguard Plate | `warden_armor_vanguard` | Armor (Epic) | 1,200 |
138	| Salute | `warden_emote_salute` | Emote | 250 |
139	| Rime Hunter | `warden_decal_rimehunter` | Decal | 300 |
140	
141	### Virtual items: boosters (consumables, priced in Cores)
142	
143	Group **Boosters**. These are consumable: granting adds a timed effect rather than a permanent unlock.
144	
145	| Name | SKU | Effect | Price (Cores) | Purchase limit |

150	
151	### Bundles
152	
153	Group **Bundles**. Show original and bundle price where a discount applies.
154	
155	**Frontier Starter Pack** (`bundle_frontier_starter`)
156	- Contents: 1,200 Cores + Obsidian (Spitter skin) + Salvage Surge (24h)
157	- Price: **$9.99 real money**

159	- Image: `assets/bundles/starter\.jpg`

162	- Contents: Huntsman + Voltaic + Ironclad + Longshot (four Rare and Epic skins)

173	- Price: **$49.99 real money**

175	- Availability window: **Season 1 only** (2026-10-14 to 2027-01-13)
176	- Image: `assets/bundles/founders\.jpg`
177	
178	### Passes and subscriptions
179	
180	Group **Passes and Subscriptions**.
181	
182	**Frontier Pass, Season 1: Cold Open** (`pass_s1_frontier`)
183	- Premium battle pass, a non-renewing one-time purchase that unlocks the season reward track.
184	- Price: **$9.99 real money**

186	- Image: `assets/passes/frontier_pass_s1\.jpg`

189	- Recurring membership.

191	- Billing period: monthly
192	- Trial period: 7 days

197	## Xsolla project configuration
198	
199	### Project setup
200	
201	- **Project name:** Voidwall
202	- **Project type:** Game
203	- **Release platforms:** Windows, macOS, iOS, Android
204	- **Storefronts:** Steam, Epic Games Store, App Store, Google Play, plus the web shop at playvoidwall.com
205	- **Monetization:** virtual currency, virtual items, bundles, subscriptions
206	- Capture the generated **Project ID**, **API key**, and **webhook secret key** for later phases.
207	
208	### Login configuration
209	
210	- **Username/password:** enabled. Password rule: min 8 characters, at least one number and one uppercase letter.
211	- **Social login:** Steam, Google, Apple, Discord.
212	- **Device ID:** enabled (mobile).
213	- **Callback URL:** https://playvoidwall.com/auth/callback
214	- **User data storage:** Xsolla-managed.
215	- **Custom user attributes:** `warden_level`, `current_season`, `lifetime_scrap`.
216	- Configure email templates for verification and password reset.
217

# Voidwall — agent context pack

This file is the single source of truth for an AI agent building a live Xsolla web shop for the fictional game *Voidwall*, by the fictional studio *Meridian Foundry*. Hand it to an agent together with the Xsolla CLI.

## How to use this file

This pack carries the decisions and data for the store: the studio, the game, the catalog, prices, and the project configuration. The agent already has the Xsolla CLI for command syntax, so this file stays focused on what to build rather than how to call it.

The agent's job: read this pack, then use the CLI to create the project, configure login and payments, build the catalog (currency, items, bundles, subscriptions), wire webhooks, and stand up the storefront. The build checklist at the end maps every section here to the Xsolla setup phases.

Image assets (item icons, currency icons, backgrounds, key art, logo) live in `./assets/` and are referenced by filename throughout. When an asset is missing, the agent should leave the image field unset and flag it.

Everything below is fiction. Use placeholder values for anything legal, financial, or personally identifying.

## The studio: Meridian Foundry

- **Studio name:** Meridian Foundry
- **Legal entity:** Meridian Foundry, Lda. (placeholder)
- **Headquarters:** Lisbon, Portugal
- **Founded:** 2021
- **Team size:** ~28 people
- **Website:** meridianfoundry.com
- **Catalog:** *Voidwall* is the studio's second title. Their first was a smaller mobile roguelike.
- **Support email:** support@playvoidwall.com
- **Brand voice:** confident, technical, a little grim. The studio talks to players like fellow engineers holding a line.

## The game: Voidwall

**Genre:** Sci-fi tower defense
**Platforms:** Windows (Steam, Epic Games Store), macOS, iOS, Android
**Player site / store domain:** playvoidwall.com

### Premise and setting

Humanity's expansion has stalled at the **Frontier**, the ragged edge of charted space. Out there drift the **Wells**: derelict alien megastructures that periodically wake and flood nearby colonies with the **Rime**, a self-replicating machine swarm that freezes and consumes everything it reaches.

Players are **Wardens**: engineers who deploy and upgrade automated turret networks across orbital platforms and colony hulls to hold the line through escalating Rime waves. The turret line players build is called the **Voidwall**.

### Core gameplay loop

1. Deploy turrets onto fixed **hardpoints** across a map.
2. Manage a **power budget**, since every turret draws energy.
3. Survive escalating waves of Rime.
4. Earn **Scrap** (soft currency) from kills and completed waves.
5. Spend Scrap and **Cores** (premium currency) to unlock, upgrade, and customize turrets between waves and runs.

### Turret classes

Six classes anchor the economy. Players unlock and field the classes through gameplay; the classes themselves are never sold. The store sells **cosmetic skins** that re-dress a class a player already fields. Skins change appearance only and carry no stat or gameplay effect, so the store stays cosmetic-only and non-pay-to-win. Each skin is its own SKU.

| Class | Role |
|-------|------|
| **Spitter** | Rapid kinetic, low cost, anti-swarm |
| **Arclight** | Chain lightning, hits multiple linked targets |
| **Bulwark** | Slow heavy cannon, high single-target damage |
| **Hailstorm** | Flak burst, area denial |
| **Lancer** | Long-range railgun, anti-armor sniper |
| **Tether** | Support field, slows and weakens enemies in range |

### Art direction (for asset generation)

Use this when generating or selecting store assets so everything stays consistent.

- **Palette:**
  - Void black `#0A0E14` (backgrounds)
  - Hull steel `#2A3242` (panels, structures)
  - Cyan energy `#35E0FF` (friendly weapons, UI accent)
  - Plasma white `#EAF6FF` (highlights, weapon glow)
  - Warning amber `#FFA63D` (alerts, legendary rarity)
  - Rime violet `#8B6CFF` (the enemy swarm)
- **Style:** clean hard-surface sci-fi, physically based rendering for in-game objects; painterly, high-contrast key art for promo. Cold, industrial, lit by weapon glow against deep space.
- **Item icons:** the item centered on a dark hexagonal tile, with a rarity-colored rim glow. Common gray, Rare blue, Epic purple, Legendary amber.
- **Logo:** wordmark `VOIDWALL` in a geometric industrial face, paired with a shield/wall glyph formed from hexagons.
- **Typography:** geometric industrial sans for display; clean humanist sans for body.

## The store

Premium currency is **Cores**, bought with real money. Soft currency is **Scrap**, earned in-game. Scrap is listed here only so the agent models it and keeps it out of the storefront.

### Item groups (catalog structure)

Create these groups in display order:

1. **Currency** — Core packages
2. **Turret Skins** — cosmetic skins per turret class
3. **Warden Gear** — player avatar cosmetics, emotes, decals
4. **Boosters** — consumable progression boosts
5. **Bundles** — multi-item value packs
6. **Passes and Subscriptions** — battle pass and recurring membership

### Currencies

| Currency | SKU | Type | Sold? | Image |
|----------|-----|------|-------|-------|
| Cores | `cores` | Premium (hard) | Yes, via packages | `assets/currency/cores\.jpg` |
| Scrap | `scrap` | Soft (earned) | No | `assets/currency/scrap\.jpg` |

### Virtual currency packages (Cores, real money)

All in group **Currency**. Prices in USD; set regional pricing per the Localization section.

| Package | SKU | Cores (base + bonus = total) | Price USD | Image |
|---------|-----|------------------------------|-----------|-------|
| Core Cache | `cores_500` | 500 + 0 = 500 | 4.99 | `assets/currency/pack_cache\.jpg` |
| Core Stack | `cores_1200` | 1,100 + 100 = 1,200 | 9.99 | `assets/currency/pack_stack\.jpg` |
| Core Crate | `cores_2600` | 2,300 + 300 = 2,600 | 19.99 | `assets/currency/pack_crate\.jpg` |
| Core Vault | `cores_7000` | 5,800 + 1,200 = 7,000 | 49.99 | `assets/currency/pack_vault\.jpg` |
| Core Reactor | `cores_15000` | 11,500 + 3,500 = 15,000 | 99.99 | `assets/currency/pack_reactor\.jpg` |

### Virtual items: turret skins (priced in Cores)

Group **Turret Skins**. Image path pattern: `assets/skins/<sku>\.jpg`.

| Name | SKU | Class | Rarity | Price (Cores) |
|------|-----|-------|--------|---------------|
| Obsidian | `spitter_skin_obsidian` | Spitter | Rare | 800 |
| Huntsman | `spitter_skin_huntsman` | Spitter | Epic | 1,500 |
| Voltaic | `arclight_skin_voltaic` | Arclight | Rare | 800 |
| Solar Flare | `arclight_skin_solarflare` | Arclight | Legendary | 2,400 |
| Ironclad | `bulwark_skin_ironclad` | Bulwark | Rare | 800 |
| Warlord | `bulwark_skin_warlord` | Bulwark | Epic | 1,500 |
| Frostbite | `hailstorm_skin_frostbite` | Hailstorm | Epic | 1,500 |
| Tempest | `hailstorm_skin_tempest` | Hailstorm | Legendary | 2,400 |
| Longshot | `lancer_skin_longshot` | Lancer | Rare | 800 |
| Deadeye | `lancer_skin_deadeye` | Lancer | Legendary | 2,400 |
| Anchor | `tether_skin_anchor` | Tether | Rare | 800 |

Set a custom attribute on each skin: `rarity` and `turret_class`.

### Virtual items: Warden gear (priced in Cores)

Group **Warden Gear**.

| Name | SKU | Type | Price (Cores) |
|------|-----|------|---------------|
| Frontier Issue | `warden_armor_frontier` | Armor (Common) | 400 |
| Vanguard Plate | `warden_armor_vanguard` | Armor (Epic) | 1,200 |
| Salute | `warden_emote_salute` | Emote | 250 |
| Rime Hunter | `warden_decal_rimehunter` | Decal | 300 |

### Virtual items: boosters (consumables, priced in Cores)

Group **Boosters**. These are consumable: granting adds a timed effect rather than a permanent unlock.

| Name | SKU | Effect | Price (Cores) | Purchase limit |
|------|-----|--------|---------------|----------------|
| Salvage Surge (24h) | `booster_salvage_24h` | 2× Scrap for 24h | 300 | 5 / day |
| Field Promotion (24h) | `booster_xp_24h` | 2× Warden XP for 24h | 300 | 5 / day |
| Salvage Surge (7 days) | `booster_salvage_7d` | 2× Scrap for 7 days | 1,200 | none |

### Bundles

Group **Bundles**. Show original and bundle price where a discount applies.

**Frontier Starter Pack** (`bundle_frontier_starter`)
- Contents: 1,200 Cores + Obsidian (Spitter skin) + Salvage Surge (24h)
- Price: **$9.99 real money**
- Purchase limit: **1 per user**
- Image: `assets/bundles/starter\.jpg`

**Warden's Arsenal** (`bundle_wardens_arsenal`)
- Contents: Huntsman + Voltaic + Ironclad + Longshot (four Rare and Epic skins)
- Price: **4,000 Cores** (individual value 4,700 Cores; show the discount)
- Image: `assets/bundles/arsenal\.jpg`

**Rime Hunter Bundle** (`bundle_rime_hunter`)
- Contents: Deadeye (Legendary Lancer skin) + Salute emote + Rime Hunter decal
- Price: **$14.99 real money**
- Image: `assets/bundles/rime_hunter\.jpg`

**Founder's Pack** (`bundle_founders`)
- Contents: Vanguard Plate + Solar Flare + Tempest + 7,000 Cores + 30 days Warden's Charter + exclusive "Plank Owner" title
- Price: **$49.99 real money**
- Purchase limit: **1 per user**
- Availability window: **Season 1 only** (2026-10-14 to 2027-01-13)
- Image: `assets/bundles/founders\.jpg`

### Passes and subscriptions

Group **Passes and Subscriptions**.

**Frontier Pass, Season 1: Cold Open** (`pass_s1_frontier`)
- Premium battle pass, a non-renewing one-time purchase that unlocks the season reward track.
- Price: **$9.99 real money**
- Availability window: **2026-10-14 to 2027-01-13**
- Image: `assets/passes/frontier_pass_s1\.jpg`

**Warden's Charter** (`sub_wardens_charter`, subscription / Phase 8)
- Recurring membership.
- Price: **$7.99 / month**
- Billing period: monthly
- Trial period: 7 days
- Grace period: 3 days
- Benefits and entitlements: 300 Cores daily stipend, 10% shop discount, one exclusive skin each month, permanent 2× Scrap while active.
- Image: `assets/passes/wardens_charter\.jpg`

## Xsolla project configuration

### Project setup

- **Project name:** Voidwall
- **Project type:** Game
- **Release platforms:** Windows, macOS, iOS, Android
- **Storefronts:** Steam, Epic Games Store, App Store, Google Play, plus the web shop at playvoidwall.com
- **Monetization:** virtual currency, virtual items, bundles, subscriptions
- Capture the generated **Project ID**, **API key**, and **webhook secret key** for later phases.

### Login configuration

- **Username/password:** enabled. Password rule: min 8 characters, at least one number and one uppercase letter.
- **Social login:** Steam, Google, Apple, Discord.
- **Device ID:** enabled (mobile).
- **Callback URL:** https://playvoidwall.com/auth/callback
- **User data storage:** Xsolla-managed.
- **Custom user attributes:** `warden_level`, `current_season`, `lifetime_scrap`.
- Configure email templates for verification and password reset.

### Payments (Pay Station)

- **Payment methods:** cards, PayPal, Apple Pay, Google Pay, plus regional methods (for example Boleto and Pix in Brazil).
- **Default currency:** USD.
- **Pay Station theme:** dark background `#0A0E14`, cyan accent `#35E0FF`, plasma-white text. Match the game's UI.

### Webhooks (backend)

- **Endpoint:** https://api.playvoidwall.com/xsolla/webhooks (HTTPS)
- Validate signatures with the webhook secret key.
- Handle: `user_validation`, `order_paid` (grant the purchased items, currency, and entitlements), `refund`, `chargeback`, and subscription lifecycle events (created, renewed, canceled, expired).

## Localization

Default locale is English (`en`). Localize names and descriptions for: `en`, `fr`, `de`, `ja`, `pt-BR`.

Provide all five across the catalog. As a worked example, the Obsidian Spitter skin:

| Locale | Name | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| en | Obsidian | A matte-black Spitter chassis cut from salvaged Well plating. |
| fr | Obsidienne | Un châssis de Spitter noir mat, taillé dans le blindage récupéré d'un Puits. |
| de | Obsidian | Ein mattschwarzes Spitter-Chassis aus geborgener Well-Panzerung. |
| ja | オブシディアン | ウェルの装甲を再利用した、つや消しブラックのスピッター機体。 |
| pt-BR | Obsidiana | Um chassi Spitter preto fosco forjado com blindagem recuperada de um Poço. |

Set regional pricing on every real-money SKU. Worked example for the Core Stack (`cores_1200`):

| Region | Currency | Price |
|--------|----------|-------|
| US | USD | 9.99 |
| Eurozone | EUR | 9.99 |
| UK | GBP | 8.99 |
| Brazil | BRL | 49.90 |
| Japan | JPY | 1,500 |

Apply equivalent regional tiers across the rest of the real-money catalog.

## Build checklist (maps to the Zero-to-Shop phases)

1. **Project setup** — create the Voidwall project; capture Project ID, API key, webhook secret.
2. **Login** — enable auth methods, social providers, device ID, callbacks, custom attributes, email templates.
3. **Catalog structure** — create the six item groups in display order.
4. **Virtual currency** — create Cores and Scrap; create the five Core packages with bonuses.
5. **Virtual items** — create all turret skins, Warden gear, and boosters; set images, prices, attributes, and purchase limits.
6. **Bundles** — create the four bundles; set contents, prices, discounts, limits, and the Founder's Pack availability window.
7. **Subscriptions** — create the Frontier Pass (non-renewing, windowed) and the Warden's Charter subscription with trial, grace, and entitlements.
8. **Payments** — configure methods, regional methods, default currency, and the Pay Station theme.
9. **Localization and regional pricing** — localize names and descriptions in five locales; set regional pricing on every real-money SKU.
10. **Storefront** — build the web shop (hero with logo and key art, login, catalog grid, featured bundles, cart with promo field, footer).
11. **Webhooks** — deploy the endpoint, set the URL, validate signatures, implement granting and lifecycle handlers.
12. **Testing** — sandbox mode, test user, full purchase and grant flows for an item, a currency pack, a bundle, and the subscription.
13. **Go live** — verify the agreement, publish the site, switch to live mode, confirm a real purchase grants correctly.

1 # Voidwall build — what didn't work as wanted 2 3 Friction log from building the Voidwall catalog + webshop via the `xsolla` CLI (dev build) against merchant `872915`, project `309336`. Grouped by severity. Each entry: symptom → impact → status/workaround. 4 5 ## Hard blockers (needed a workaround or manual step) 6 7 1. **Couldn't create the project from the CLI.** 8 - `merchant create-projects` with the project-level API key → **401** (that key doesn't authenticate the legacy merchant API at all, reads included). 9 - With the merchant-level key → **422 "Serverless integration is available only for projects with tokenless integration"** — an account-level rule the create payload can't override (the CLI sends a clean `{"name":...}`). 10 - `publisher create-project` → needs a keychain login (`xsolla publisher login`); it ignores `XSOLLA_TOKEN`, so it can't run headlessly ("not configured"). 11 - **Status:** project created manually in Publisher Account UI; ID `309336` handed back. 12 13 2. **Bulk catalog import is forbidden for this account.** 14 - `catalog import-admin-catalog` → **403 "Requested endpoint is forbidden"**, even though ordinary catalog writes (currencies, packages) succeed with the same key. 15 - **Impact:** the one-shot, full-fidelity catalog import (the only CLI path that carries `vc_prices`/groups/attributes/types in one call) is unavailable. 16 - **Status:** worked around per-entity; rich item fields ultimately dropped from CLI-only scope. 17 18 3. **Item images cannot be set.** — ✅ **RESOLVED** (a newer CLI build added `shopbuilder upload-asset` / `list-assets` / `delete-asset`). 19 - `upload-asset --type image --file --landing-id ` uploads to the Xsolla CDN and returns the public HTTPS URL, which works as both a block image and a catalog `image_url`. 20 - **Done:** page background, hero logo, hero key-art uploaded and wired into the site; 4 of 5 Core packages now have card thumbnails (set via GET-merge-PUT on the admin API, since the typed package update has no `--image-url` flag). 21 - **Custom-generated icon:** No image-generation tool here, but authored a Power Core **SVG** (`assets/currency/cores_svg.svg`) and rasterized it via Inkscape → `sips` to a 280×280 JPEG (`assets/currency/cores_svg.jpg`), then set it on the **Cores currency** and the **Core Reactor** package (`cores_15000`, which had no source file `pack_reactor.jpg`). Reactor ideally still wants its own "reactor chamber" art, but now shows a quality core icon instead of the plain placeholder. Skin/gear/bundle images are pending only because those items aren't built yet. 22 23 ## CLI capability gaps 24 25 4. **Typed `catalog create-items` / `update-items` are too thin for real items.** 26 - No flags for: `vc_prices` (Cores pricing), group assignment, `attributes` (rarity/turret_class), `virtual_item_type` (consumable vs not), `image_url`, or limits-on-create. 27 - **Impact:** the entire cosmetic catalog (skins, gear, boosters) and bundles can't be built correctly through the CLI's typed surface — only currencies and currency packages map cleanly. 28 29 5. **Shop Builder `create-website` only supports `--type topup`.** 30 - No other landing type is creatable from the CLI. (A topup landing *can* still hold blocks, which wasn't obvious at first.) 31 32 6. **`shopbuilder verify-website` → 404** on the topup landing — readiness check unavailable, couldn't verify publish-readiness programmatically. 33 34 ## Quirks / gotchas (cost time, work once understood) 35 36 7. **`update-block` silently no-ops if the patch path omits `values`.** 37 - Block patches must use `["values", ...]`; site patches use document-root paths (`["theme", ...]`). A wrong-rooted block patch returns `ok:true` but changes nothing — no error. Burned one full round. 38 39 8. **Authored block text isn't visible in `get-structure`.** 40 - Block titles/descriptions/FAQ are stored as `L:` localization ids; the structure shows only the id, not the text. Can't confirm copy from the structure — have to trust the freshly-generated id or check the preview. 41 42 9. **Inconsistent flags across `shopbuilder` subcommands.** 43 - `enable-preview` / `preview-link` reject `--merchant-id`/`--project-id` (slug-only), while sibling commands require them. 44 - `move-block` uses `--source`/`--destination` (indices), not `--blockid`/`--index`. 45 46 10. **`add-block` ordering races.** Sequential adds landed out of order (FAQ before Store); had to `move-block` to fix the sequence. 47 48 11. **Fresh landing structure was momentarily empty.** First `get-structure` returned `pages:[] / blocks:[]`; the 11 default template blocks appeared on a later fetch. Misleading initial read. 49 50 11b. **Block `background.color` is a tint *over* the image, not a fallback behind it.** Setting it to an opaque value (e.g. `rgba(10,14,20,1)`) paints a solid layer on top and **hides the background image entirely** — the image only appeared after manually toggling "tint" in the editor (which drops the color to low opacity). Fix: set `background.color` to a low-alpha tint (e.g. `rgba(10,14,20,0.2)`) or transparent, and do the darkening with `background.gradient`. The editor also normalizes the descriptor on save (adds `player`/`video` keys), which a raw API patch doesn't. 51 52 12. **Virtual currency create demands a default price when shown in store.** Direct POST of `cores` with `is_show_in_store` → **422 "Item default price not set"**. Worked around by creating it via the CLI's minimal body (premium currency is sold via packages, not directly, so this is fine). 53 54 ## Left incomplete / not to spec 55 56 13. **Catalog is partial.** — ✅ **RESOLVED.** Full catalog now built via the admin API: 11 turret skins (Cores-priced, with `rarity`/`turret_class` attributes), 5 Warden gear items (incl. the bundle-only "Plank Owner" title), 3 boosters (consumable, 24h/7d), 4 bundles, and the Frontier Pass — all with images. Plus the earlier currencies, 5 Core packages, and the Warden's Charter subscription. 57 58 13a. **Bundles can't be priced in virtual currency.** The bundle admin endpoint **silently drops `vc_prices`** (create returns 201, update 204, but the price never persists). Warden's Arsenal was specced at 4,000 Cores; converted to the real-money equivalent **$29.99** (by the Core-package rate) so it's actually sellable. Real-money bundles (Starter/Rime Hunter/Founder's) work fine. 59 60 13b. **Item purchase-limit endpoint is forbidden** (403, same class as the import endpoint). Worked around by setting `limits` inside the item body via GET-merge-PUT — boosters 5/day (`recurrent_schedule` daily), Starter & Founder's 1/user. 61 62 13c. **Booster `inventory_options.consumable` must be a boolean** on create (`true`), not the `{usages_count}` object the GET/import shape shows. 422 until corrected. 63 64 14. **Storefront now shows the full catalog** (6 groups populated), not just the Core packages. 65 66 14e. **Block text must be HTML, not plain strings.** Authoring block text (titles, descriptions, FAQ, section titles) with bare strings in the `localizedString` map renders in an unstyled "plain text" style. The editor and default fields store HTML (e.g. `

…

`). Re-authored every text field wrapped in `

`. `get-structure` doesn't inline localized text — verify via the `update-block` response's `localizations.map`. 67 68 14b. **Store block shipped with template placeholder sections** — including a literal `__test__/bundle` group showing test data. The `newStore` block's sections live in its `components[]` array (`section.item.group` + `section.item.type`), not in `values`. Re-pointed all sections to the Voidwall groups and added Boosters/Passes sections (cloned a component, new `_id`, appended via `add` patch). 69 70 14c. **Currency packages aren't shown by group.** A `bundle`-type section on the `currency` group returns 0. Packages surface through the dedicated currency-packages endpoint and render via a `virtual_currency` (top-up) section with group `__all__` — packages carry no group in the working reference (turbo-clicker). Section types are `virtual_currency` / `virtual_good` / `bundle`. 71 72 14d. **Future-dated items are hidden (correct, not a bug).** The Frontier Pass and Founder's Pack use the Season 1 window `2026-10-14 → 2027-01-13`; with today before that, the storefront hides them, so the Passes section is empty until the season opens. 73 74 14a. **Site theme reverted to the generic default** (purple accent, lime-green secondary, round buttons) at some point between the first patch and later editor activity — had to re-apply the brand theme. Suggests editor sessions and API patches can clobber each other on the theme object; re-verify the theme after any editor work. 75 76 15. **Regional pricing is approximate.** EUR mapped only to DE/FR (other eurozone countries fall back to USD conversion); BRL/JPY computed by multiplier, so minor divergence from the context's worked example (e.g. BRL 49.95 vs. the spec's 49.90). 77 78 16. **Package descriptions are English-only** (e.g. "1,200 Cores."); only names + the storefront block copy got the full 5-locale treatment. 79 80 ## Environment noise (not Voidwall-specific) 81 82 17. **Xsolla MCP (`search_xsolla_sources`) intermittently failed** with "Unable to connect" — retries worked. 83 84 18. **Two `xsolla` binaries on the machine.** `~/.local/bin/xsolla` is the **dev** build (has `shopbuilder upload-asset`, asset commands, corrected flags); `/opt/homebrew/bin/xsolla` is an older release that lacks them ("unknown flag: --merchant-id" on `upload-asset`). Forcing `/opt/homebrew/bin` to the front of `PATH` shadowed the dev build and silently used the wrong one. Fix: call the dev binary by absolute path, or keep `~/.local/bin` ahead in `PATH`. 85 86 --- 87 *Generated 2026-06-25. Catalog/site live in sandbox project `309336`; webshop slug `voidwall` (preview enabled).* 88
